•	 We upgraded our view on US equities from slightly underweight to neutral. An important consideration 
for us is to what extent AI could boost corporate earnings and how much of a valuation premium is 
justified for such businesses. 
•	 While we believe in the long-term potential for such technology to enhance productivity, we are

Europe
Slightly Overweight
•	 We have moved our positioning from overweight to slightly overweight on European equities. 
•	 Trade policy risks remain a concern, but targeted fiscal and monetary measures could help mitigate 
their impact.
•	 While high valuations and market concentration in the US argue for diversifying into other regions 
such as Europe, a weaker US dollar could weigh on exporters’ earnings, so we are adopting a slightly 
more cautious stance. 
Japan
Slightly Overweight
•	 Ongoing buybacks and robust dividend policies are evidence of improving corporate governance. 
Corporate governance and structural reform remain important drivers for the market. 
•	 Valuations are relatively attractive and offer useful diversification away from a concentrated US 
market. Recent political developments further raise the prospect of additional fiscal support, 
reinforcing our modestly positive stance.
Asia Pacific  
ex-Japan
Slightly Overweight
•	 We remain slightly overweight on Asia Pacific equities. Expectations of a weaker US dollar and a 
stronger growth premium versus developed markets support a broadly constructive view of the 
region.
•	 We are positive on India. Recent policy measures point to a shift toward more supportive — for 
example, proposed tax cuts in the 2026 budget, GST rate revisions, and increased farmer income 
support. This broader fiscal tilt, combined with historically low inflation supporting real incomes 
and scope for Reserve Bank of India easing.
•	 In South Korea, the ongoing “value up” program should sustain momentum, but stocks have rerated 
materially and no longer look cheap. In Taiwan, expensive equities valuations justify a slightly more 
cautious stance.
•	 The ASEAN region offers relatively attractive valuations and dividend support but lacks strong near 
term catalysts.
China & Hong Kong
Neutral
•	 We maintain a neutral stance on China and Hong Kong equities.
•	 Sentiment has improved — supported by ongoing tariff negotiations, positive tech-sector 
developments and relatively attractive valuations — but we remain cautious given persistent 
overcapacity in several industries.
•	 We expect growth to slow but remain sufficient for authorities to avoid large-scale fiscal stimulus, 
so an immediate policy-driven catalyst is unlikely.

Neutral

Neutral
We are neutral on government bonds, with a neutral duration stance in both the US and Europe.
•	 UK duration is our highest-conviction view within government bonds, as leading indicators remain 
consistent with a softer labour market.
•	 In Japan we remain negative on duration amid BoJ rate hikes expectation.
•	 In Asia, lower US Treasury yields are providing broad support to local bond markets, although we 
are watching political and social developments in Indonesia and their potential impact on sovereign 
debt.

Slightly Overweight
•	 We remain slightly positive on corporate credit. Prospective central bank rate cuts should increase 
the attractiveness of income generation in credit markets, but investors must be selective given 
current valuations and credit quality dispersion. 
•	 In Euro investment grade (IG), spreads have tightened but we still see room for some compression

•	 In the US, we are neutral on IG credit due to expensive valuations and remain cautious on lower-

•	 In Asia, we expect spreads to continue grinding tighter amid a strong technical backdrop and

Global Equities and Bonds Rallied in October; 
Driven by Strong Quarterly Earnings and  
Continued Rate Cut

EUROPEAN EQUITIES
US EQUITIES
The US S&P 500 rose 2.3% in October. Early in the month, rising 
US-China tensions over export restrictions on rare earths triggered 
the S&P 500’s largest one‑day drop since April’s Liberation Day. 
However, as the month progressed, investor expectations shifted 
toward a lower likelihood of additional tariffs, and equities received 
further support from generally positive third‑quarter earnings. 
Over 82% of S&P 500 companies have beaten markets’ earnings 
estimates. Among other US indices, the Dow Jones Industrial 
Average rose 2.5%. Tech stocks experienced a positive month and 
generally led the US equity advance with the Nasdaq Composite 
rise by 4.7%.
On the macroeconomic front, the annual headline inflation rate in 
the US rose to 3% in September from 2.9% in August. Energy led 
the increase registering its largest monthly rise since May 2024 
and prices for new vehicles also picked up modestly. By contrast, 
inflation slowed for food and transportation services. However, the 
annual core inflation slowed to 3% from 3.1%. Export sales fell for 
the fourth month running, and business confidence slipped to its 
weakest level since April as firms cited concerns about global trade 
and policy uncertainty.
In terms of monetary policy, at its October meeting, the Federal 
Reserve cut the federal funds rate by 25bps to a target range 
of 3.75%–4.00%, broadly in line with market expectations. 
Policymakers noted rising downside risks to employment in recent 
months, while inflation has moved up since earlier in the year and 
remains somewhat elevated.
AI capex in the US will boost US growth, resilient consumption in 
historical data so far, along with a potential lift from capex, has 
allowed us to upgrade US growth forecasts for 2025 (1.9%) and 
2026 (1.9%). However, AI capex would be unable to completely 
offset the decline in consumption, which remains the mainstay 
of the US economy, as well as labour markets remaining weak, 
leading us to conclude that the broader weakening trend doesn’t 
change. Investment in the tech sector has not yet resulted in 
massive creation of new jobs and is unlikely to boost job markets 
in the near term.
Whilst the Fed communication has somewhat downplayed the 
probability of a December cut because of the resilient activity and 
sticky inflation, we believe the Fed will also consider the profile 
with rising unemployment and weakening labour market. Hence, 
we expected that FED would likely do so one more time this year 
and twice next.
Although we upgraded our view on US equities from slightly 
underweight to neutral, an important consideration for us is to 
what extent AI could boost corporate earnings and how much of 
a valuation premium is justified for such businesses. While we 
believe in the long-term potential for such technology to enhance 
productivity, we are unwilling to pay excessive valuations.
•	 We remain slightly overweight on US value equities, as provide a 
good balance of earnings, valuations and product differentiation.
•	 We are moving our view on US growth equities to slightly 
underweight, supported by resilient US earnings and strong 
capital expenditure commitments aimed at boosting productivity 
and competitiveness. However, we remain cautious overall given 
elevated market concentration, rich valuations, and ongoing 
uncertainty about the sustainability of the capex cycle and its 
ability to generate monetisable returns.
In Europe, markets broadly followed the positive global trend, but returns 
were initially affected by political noise in France and limited exposure to 
commodities and AI related tech names: the MSCI Europe advanced 2.5% 
in local terms. After a relatively flat first half of the month, France’s CAC 
40 finished the month up 2.9% , as Prime Minister S. Lecornu won the 
crucial support of the Socialist Party in the National Assembly, fuelling 
optimism for a more stable political outlook. In the UK, the market was 
supported by a fall in gilt yields and commodity strength. A weaker pound 
also lifted returns by increasing the sterling value of overseas earnings. 
The FTSE 100 index rose 4.1% in total return terms.
On the macroeconomic front, the Eurozone economy expanded by 
0.2% q/q in Q3, up from 0.1% in Q2, according to a flash estimate. At 
country level, France grew 0.5% driven by a sharp rise in exports, while 
Spain remained the best performer among the bloc’s largest economies, 
expanding 0.6% supported by strong household consumption and fixed 
investment. Meanwhile, Germany stagnated due to a decline in exports, 
and Italy stalled, with the industrial sector contracting and services 
showing no growth. Regarding inflation, the inflation rate in the Euro Area 
eased to 2.1% in October, in line with market expectations and down from 
2.2% in September.
On the monetary policy front, the ECB left interest rates unchanged at 2% 
for a third consecutive meeting in October. The central bank reiterated its 
policy approach: decisions will be data dependent with no commitment 
to a particular rate path. The ECB Vice President Luis de Guindos 
judged that any dip in inflation below 2% would likely be temporary, and 
premature easing could reignite price pressures, especially given higher 
wage settlements in France and Spain.
On the monetary policy front, as the Federal Reserve pursues a more 
aggressive rate-cutting cycle than the ECB, an appreciating EUR/USD 
exchange rate, combined with US tariffs, would place additional pressure 
on EU exports and, ultimately, on economic growth. In this context, we 
expect the European Central Bank to implement one additional rate cut 
this year and one in the first half of 2026. For the Bank of England, we 
think the bank will reduce policy rates in December this year.
While high valuations and market concentration in the US argue for 
diversifying into other regions such as Europe, a weaker US dollar could 
weigh on exporters’ earnings, so we are adopting a slightly more cautious 
stance. Trade-policy risks remain a concern, although targeted fiscal and 
monetary measures could help mitigate their impact. Our assessment 
points to downside in the near term and beginning of the following year 
due to potential delays to and adjustments in the German fiscal stimulus 
and pressures on exports. But resilience in economic activity in Spain 
and Italy would continue. The latest US sanctions on Russia indicate that 
the former is more likely to be aligned with the EU on security challenges. 
Any indications of a ceasefire with Ukraine (still elusive) would be 
positive for the European economy and assets. It is expected that Euro 
Area growth will likely slow this year, and then pick up from mid-2026, still 
below the long-term trend. Hence, we have moved our positioning from 
overweight to slightly overweight on European equities but continue to 
favour UK equities within the region as elevated dividend yields, attractive 
valuations and the market’s defensive characteristics make UK stocks an 
effective portfolio diversifier.

JAPANESE EQUITIES
ASIA PACIFIC EX-JAPAN EQUITIES
In October, the Nikkei and the Topix gained 16.7% and 6.2% 
respectively. Sanae Takaichi became leader of the Liberal 
Democratic Party and was viewed by investors as likely to 
pursue more expansionary fiscal and monetary policies—an 
outlook that, together with a weaker yen, supported Japan’s 
export-oriented firms.
On the macroeconomic front, manufacturing PMI fell to 48.3 
in October, the largest decline since March 2024 and the 
steepest contraction in factory orders in 20 months, driven 
by soft business condition and weaker customer demand. 
Regarding inflation, the annual inflation climbed to 2.9%, 
reflecting persistent price pressure as energy subsidies were 
removed. However, the Bank of Japan signalled the prospect 
of slower hikes and kept its short-term policy rate unchanged 
at 0.5%.
On monetary policy, the weaker yen reinforces the case for 
additional BoJ tightening because it raises import-related 
price pressures; we see scope for one further rate hike this 
year and another in 2026 while inflation remains above the 2% 
target and we believe that JPY is likely to mean-revert after the 
extreme cheap valuation.
We remain slightly positive on Japanese equities. Ongoing 
buybacks and robust dividend policies are evidence of 
improving corporate governance. Corporate governance and 
structural reform remain important drivers for the market, 
although the Bank of Japan’s recent decision to sell ETFs is 
a countervailing factor. The exit from deflation, together with 
ongoing reforms, is supporting a stronger domestic backdrop; 
we expect GDP growth to settle around 1.3% in 2025. Recent 
political developments also increase the likelihood of further 
fiscal expansion. Under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Japan 
is likely to shift toward a more supportive fiscal stance. The 
next supplementary budget is expected to include tax relief 
(for example on gasoline), targeted exemptions and subsidies 
for energy costs, measures that could provide a meaningful 
boost to domestic consumption and act as a catalyst for 
equities. More importantly, valuations are relatively attractive 
and offer useful diversification away from a concentrated 
US market. Recent political developments further raise the 
prospect of additional fiscal support, reinforcing our modestly 
positive stance.
Asian equity markets delivered another strong month of 
performance, with the MSCI AC Asia Pacific ex-Japan rising 
4.5% in October. Renewed interest in AI and improved US-China 
trade relationships benefited most Asian markets. Among the 
developed Asian markets, the Australian All-Share Index rose 
0.5% while the Singaporean Straits Times rose 3.0%. Within 
Asian emerging markets, improvement in trade developments 
helped to support the sentiment of export-heavy economies 
particularly in the technology sector. The Korean KOSPI 
gained 19.9% and the Taiwan TWSE adding 9.3%. Elsewhere, 
India announced capital market reforms and strategic metals 
investment, the Nifty 50 returned 4.5% over the month.
On the monetary policy front, Australia’s central bank left its 
benchmark interest rate unchanged in a widely expected move 
but warned that third-quarter inflation could be stronger than 
anticipated and future decisions will depend on incoming 
economic data. The Bank of Korea kept the benchmark policy 
unchanged. The central bank extended the pause due to 
steady inflation and a better growth outlook; while noting it is 
watching housing-market stability and household debt. Bank 
Indonesia (BI) surprised the market by pausing rate cut after 
previously cutting 25 basis points in each of the past three 
meetings to support growth. The central bank will now assess 
the effectiveness of previous cuts and maintain the stability of 
the rupiah, while still leaving the door open for future rate cuts.
We remain slightly overweight on Asia Pacific equities. 
Expectations of a weaker US dollar and a stronger growth 
premium versus developed markets support a broadly 
constructive view of the region. Trade activity has held up 
despite earlier tariff concerns, and subdued inflation allowed 
many Asian central banks to adopt an easing bias; however, 
the scope for further easing is narrowing as inflation becomes 
better anchored. Earnings forecasts for the region remain 
broadly positive, while technical and sentiment are supportive. 
Valuations continue to look attractive relative to developed 
markets, but performance has been uneven, so careful stock 
and country selection is essential.
•	 We are positive on India. The market has lagged the 
broader region this year, weighed by tariff concerns and 
softer nominal GDP growth, but recent policy measures 
point to a shift toward more inclusive household support 
— for example, proposed tax cuts in the 2026 budget, GST 
rate revisions, and increased farmer income support. This 
broader fiscal tilt, combined with historically low inflation 
supporting real incomes and scope for Reserve Bank of India 
easing, underpins our constructive view.
•	 In South Korea, the ongoing “value-up” program should 
sustain momentum and act as a tailwind for equities. Robust 
corporate earnings, growing tightness in memory supply in 
the AI space as well as strengthening relationships with the 
US should continue to provide support. That said, we are 
mindful that Korean stocks have rerated materially and no 
longer look cheap.
•	 In Taiwan, expensive valuations justify a slightly more 
cautious stance.
•	 The ASEAN region offers relatively attractive valuations and 
dividend support and stands to benefit from coordinated 
easing by major central banks. However, the region still lacks 
strong near-term catalysts compared with other parts of 
APAC, and earnings revisions remain relatively muted.

Investment involves risks. Past performance is not 
indicative of future performance. The value of 
constituent funds may fall as well as rise. For further 
information about the risks involved, please refer to 
the MPF Scheme Brochure of relevant MPF Schemes.
The information contained in this document is 
provided for information purpose only and does not 
constitute any solicitation and offering of investment 
products. Potential investors should be aware that 
such investments involve market risk and should be 
regarded as long-term investments.

CHINA & HONG KONG EQUITIES
Initial concerns on the trade development between US and China 
weighed on investors’ sentiment at the start of the month. However, 
as trade talks turned more positive, markets have recovered some 
grounds and the onshore Shanghai Composite advanced 1.9% 
over the month whilst the offshore Hong Kong Hang Seng fell 
-3.5%. In particular, the offshore market was negatively impacted 
by a shrink of foreign flows into China-related stocks, decreasing 
by -52% on a month-on-month basis.
On the macroeconomic front, the Chinese economy expanded 
by 4.8% on a year-on-year basis in the third quarter. In addition, 
China witnessed the quickest industrial output pace since June, 
rising by 6.5% year-on-year in September powered by stronger 
manufacturing activity. However, retail sales growth eased slightly 
to 3%. The recently concluded 4th Plenum set priorities for the next 
five years, emphasising the development of a modern industrial 
system, technological self-reliance, strategic autonomy in key 
technologies and more resilient domestic supply chains. These 
goals are likely to shape policy choices going forward.
In terms of monetary policy, China kept the benchmark lending 
rates unchanged in October, aligned with expectations. However, 
the People’s Bank of China said they will resume open-market 
trading of treasury bonds after suspending such operations in 
December 2024. The suspension had been intended to ease 
imbalances in bond supply and demand and reduce market risk. 
The central bank will also maintain a supportive, moderately loose 
monetary stance and use various tools to provide liquidity. As a 
result of the above indications, markets have generally reacted 
positively. The People’s Bank of China stands ready to provide 
further easing if renewed trade tensions with the US create 
excessive volatility or materially weaken activity.
We maintain a neutral stance on China and Hong Kong 
equities. Sentiment has improved — supported by ongoing tariff 
negotiations, positive tech-sector developments and relatively 
attractive valuations — but we remain cautious given persistent 
overcapacity in several industries. Chinese growth is slowing but 
at a milder pace than previously expected, as recent data show. 
We have modestly upgraded our forecasts and now expect GDP 
growth of around 4.9% in 2025 and 4.4% in 2026. Because growth 
will be close to the government’s target, we do not anticipate a 
major, broad-based fiscal stimulus. Any targeted fiscal or monetary 
support will likely be conditional on how US trade policy evolves 
toward China. Overall, persistent “anti-involution” dynamics, weak 
domestic consumption and a contraction in housing investment 
imply activity will remain subdued in the near term. That said, 
authorities’ efforts to manage the rally and provide targeted 
support are constructive and could help sustain further gains. We 
continue to prefer the domestic on-shore market, which offers 
more attractive valuations and lower direct exposure to trade-
related uncertainty.
GLOBAL BONDS
Global government bonds delivered positive returns in October, 
although overall performance was held back by rising yields after the 
Fed signalled that further easing was not assured. The Federal Reserve 
cut the federal funds rate by 25bps to a target range of 3.75%–4.00%, 
broadly in line with market expectations. Policymakers noted rising 
downside risks to employment in recent months, while inflation has 
moved up since earlier in the year and remains somewhat elevated, 
hence the cautious tone on further easing. Overall, the ICE BofA US 
Government Bond Index gained 0.6%. On the other hand, The ICE BofA 
Euro Government Bond Index returned 0.9%. The ECB left interest 
rates unchanged at 2% for a third consecutive meeting in October. ECB 
reiterated its policy approach: decisions will be data dependent with no 
commitment to a particular rate path.
In Asia, the Bloomberg Asia Local Currency Bond Index retracted -0.8% 
in local currency terms but delivered 0.4% in USD terms. However 
onshore China bonds benefited from the supportive stance from the 
central bank, delivering a positive return of 0.5%.
Credit markets were relatively calm, largely following moves in 
government and swap markets. The iTraxx Main index tightened 
slightly to 55 basis points from 56 at the prior month-end. Corporate 
credit returns were modest: the Bloomberg Euro Aggregate Corporate 
Index was up 0.7% for the month, while the Bloomberg US Aggregate 
Corporate Index recorded a 0.4% gain.
Overall, we main neutral stance on Global Bond. Consumption 
pressures in the US may affect economic activity there as effects of 
US tariffs materialise. On the other hand, while inflation expectations 
are still under control, an expansionary fiscal policy, a Fed inclined to 
cut rates and US tariffs passthrough to inflation in the real economy 
may change that. Hence, curves will steepen further. In Europe, inflation 
doesn’t seem to be an issue, but domestic demand could be.
We are neutral on government bonds, with a neutral duration stance in 
both the US and Europe. With political uncertainty in France receding, 
we will look for opportunities to reduce our cautious positioning there. 
UK duration is our highest-conviction view within government bonds, 
as leading indicators remain consistent with a softer labour market. In 
Japan we remain negative on duration amid BoJ rate hikes expectation. 
In Asia, lower US Treasury yields are providing broad support to 
local bond markets, although we are watching political and social 
developments in Indonesia and their potential impact on sovereign 
debt.
We remain slightly positive on corporate credit. Prospective central- 
bank rate cuts should increase the attractiveness of income generation 
in credit markets, but investors must be selective given current 
valuations and credit quality dispersion. In euro investment-grade (IG), 
spreads have tightened but we still see room for some compression 
and fundamentals remain robust. We favour shorter term issuance and 
higher quality credits, which should benefit from limited supply and 
disciplined balance sheet management.
•	 In the US, we are neutral on IG credit due to expensive valuations 
and remain cautious on lower-quality segments. Given stretched 
valuations and a recent broader AI skepticism, issuers with weaker 
balance sheets and concentrated AI exposure are not our preferred 
names across fixed income strategies.
•	 In the Eurozone, we remain positive on EU IG as corporate 
fundamentals remain strong but stay neutral on the high yield 
segment.
•	 In Asia, we expect spreads to continue grinding tighter amid a strong 
technical backdrop and maintain a preference for high-quality credit.
